extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, reformers, and policymakers interested in political philosophy and constitutional design (readers of Mill's political theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for choosing, adapting, and judging forms of government—with emphasis on representative government and the social, moral, and mechanical conditions that make particular institutions suitable or effective. Draws on practical examples and warnings about anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three fundamental conditions for adaptation of forms of government
rubrics_metrics.description: The people for whom the form of government is intended must (1) be willing to accept it (or not so unwilling as to oppose its establishment), (2) be willing and able to do what is necessary to keep it standing, and (3) be willing and able to do what it requires of them to enable it to fulfill its purposes (the word 'do' includes forbearances as well as acts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill states that 'the failure of any of these conditions renders a form of government, whatever favorable promise it may otherwise hold out, unsuitable to the particular case.' Use these three conditions as a gatekeeping test before attempting to transplant or implement institutions. Examples and anti-patterns (below) illustrate practical failures of each condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular acceptance / absence of repugnance
rubrics_metrics.description: A form of government is unsuitable where the people are repugnant to it; nothing short of foreign force can impose such an alien polity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill gives examples (e.g., North American tribes, certain nations preferring family rule) to show that if a people will not voluntarily submit, attempts to impose the form are impracticable. Consider cultural attachments and historical loyalties when proposing reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity and willingness to preserve the government (defense and endurance)
rubrics_metrics.description: People must be willing and able to preserve the government—e.g., fight for it if attacked, not be deluded out of it, and resist panics or cults of personality that cede liberties to a single individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns include indolence, carelessness, cowardice, or susceptibility to demagoguery. Mill warns that a people unable to defend or maintain a free government are 'more or less unfit for liberty' and that short-lived freedom may be harmful if not sustained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic forbearance and cooperation with law enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: A people must be capable of the forbearances and cooperative acts required by civilized government—refraining from private vengeance and assisting public authorities in repression of crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill cites behaviors (perjury to shield criminals, bystanders ignoring public violence, being revolted by executions but not assassinations) as signs that stronger, more despotic powers may be needed. Gauge public moral habits and public trust in law before relying on institutions that assume civic cooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral engagement and independence of suffrage
rubrics_metrics.description: Representative institutions are valuable only when electors are sufficiently interested in government to vote on public grounds; they should not sell votes or vote at the beck of patrons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the electorate is apathetic or controlled (votes sold, influenced by patrons), elections can become 'an additional wheel' in machinery of misgovernment. Evaluate the integrity and independence of voting behavior when judging representative systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical/administrative capacity for public opinion and governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical and administrative conditions (e.g., means of communication like the press, capacity to collect taxes and maintain forces) are necessary to form and propagate public opinion and to exercise authority over large territories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill argues that without physical conditions for public opinion (the 'Pnyx' equivalent—newspaper press) or administrative reach (taxation, army fidelity), certain forms (regulated popular government, monarchy over large territories) cannot function effectively. Assess infrastructure and communication as part of suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of social power and the role of active opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Government tends to reflect the strongest active social forces, but 'power' must include active organization and opinion; belief and organized moral conviction are major components of social power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate mere possession of property or numbers with political determinism: organized, active forces (including intellectual conviction) can change constitutions. Mill emphasizes acting on opinion as a means to alter the balance of power—so measure both material resources and the state of public convictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: The aggregate interests of society as the test of good government
rubrics_metrics.description: The criterion of a good form of government is its conduciveness to the aggregate interests of society—its ability to promote the whole range of human well-being rather than any narrow function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill rejects treating government as merely for 'Order' or merely for 'Progress' alone; both preservation and improvement of social good are interlinked. Evaluate governments by their total effect on social welfare, not just by narrow metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government should foster civic virtues: industry, integrity, justice, prudence
rubrics_metrics.description: The qualities in citizens that preserve existing good—industry, integrity, justice, prudence—are also those that promote improvement; a government's excellence includes promoting these virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies and institutions should be judged by how they encourage these dispositions. Mill argues that agencies that cultivate these virtues both preserve and advance society; measure laws and institutions by their moral-educative effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government should encourage activity, enterprise, courage, and originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualities associated more with Progress—mental activity, enterprise, courage, originality—are also necessary for permanence because maintenance of gains requires ongoing energy and invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good government stimulates energy and invention; assess whether institutions allow and reward initiative and adaptation, since stagnation endangers retained gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of police and law enforcement (security of person and property)
rubrics_metrics.description: A system of policing that represses crime and secures person and property promotes both Order and Progress by releasing individuals' faculties for productive and cooperative endeavors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the police example to evaluate how enforcement institutions contribute indirectly to economic production, social trust, and moral education. A capable, just police promotes broader social improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound taxation and financial administration
rubrics_metrics.description: A good system of taxation and finance should be economical, distribute burdens justly, not impede industry, and foster moral example in difficult adjustments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill notes that sound finance both preserves national wealth and encourages creation of more; evaluate fiscal institutions for economy, fairness, and their effects on industry and public morality.
